results.title: Filipinos in Israel
results.description: First of two parts AILEEN Mendiola, the ambassador of the Philippines to Israel, sits across from me in the holding area of a restaurant in Tel Aviv. It’s a warm night in August, and peals of laughter could be heard from the other room where other Filipino journalists are waiting to interview the ambassador. The ambassador, who trained as an academic, has been in the diplomatic service since 1993. “I don’t do creative writing like you do, Danton, but I was quite good with feasibility studies and project management,” she told me. Streaks of gray and white dominate her bob cut. She was wearing a white top and colorful native garb that looked like an elegant tapis, but made of thicker material. “I studied history at the university and specialized in Chinese culture, which led me to pursue further studies in both Taiwan and mainland China through a scholarship from our foreign ministry. I served at the Philippine mission in China and worked at the Office of the President during the Ramos administration, where I gained invaluable experience. Later, I was posted in Singapore with a portfolio spanning economic, political and cultural affairs. I then spent nine enriching years in Shanghai as consul general, including overseeing the Philippine pavilion at the World Expo.” After that, she was posted to Paris as deputy ambassador and focused on political and security issues, as well as represented the Philippines at Unesco. Before coming to Israel, she served as the director-general for the Asia-Pacific region, managing our relations with 44 countries. One of her top priorities is strengthening economic ties and fostering joint business ventures. “I’m keen to encourage two-way investment: Israeli businesses entering the Philippine market, and Filipino enterprises exploring opportunities in Israel. I’m deeply impressed by Israeli innovation and technology, and I’m actively exploring ways to bring some of that expertise to the Philippines.” She is also focused on opening the door wider for Filipinos who want to work as caregivers in Israel by amending the labor agreement between the two countries. She doesn’t want our caregivers to be mired in debt even before they leave the Philippines. Currently, Israel hires a third-party provider to process the documentation of our caregivers. She wants to do away with the services of this provider that the applicants pay for even before leaving the Philippines, like a Covid-19 screening. One upshot of this is that the expenses for this third-party provider are borne by our caregivers, who need to pay up front before they leave, and even a month after they arrive. So, the ambassador gathered together several ambassadors from countries that have caregivers in Israel and wrote a pooled letter to the Israeli government for the amendment of the labor agreement. However, there has been no response so far. Culturally, the ambassador would like to see more artistic and historical exchange between our countries. “One personal dream of mine is to bring the Dead Sea Scrolls to the Philippines for a museum exhibition. Beyond that, there’s an important piece of shared history I wish to highlight: during the Holocaust, when nearly every country closed its borders to Jewish refugees, the Philippines stood alone in opening its doors.” Under the leadership of President Manuel Luis Quezon, thousands of Jewish refugees found a safe haven in the Philippines. Quezon even donated his private land to help them resettle. “I hope to work with Yad Vashem to have him be officially recognized as Righteous Among the Nations and to raise broader awareness of this remarkable act of humanity.” “While President Quezon has been recognized locally, there is still a need to create meaningful, tangible connections through tourism and public engagement. We are exploring several initiatives to bring his legacy to life. This includes a ‘Quezon Day’ at the embassy, which is a day dedicated to community activities such as sports events and the screening of a documentary about President Quezon’s humanitarian efforts. “We also need to have educational programs in schools. This includes presentations, lectures and interactive sessions to introduce students to this inspiring chapter in history. Following the recent inauguration of the Quezon Memorial in Rishon LeZion, we are considering the establishment of a museum that would feature stories and artifacts from that era, deepening public understanding and engagement.” I visited the Quezon memorial in Rishon LeZion, which was set in a lush garden, similar to other green gardens in Israel. It features a sculptural work similar to the Quezon Memorial Circle in Quezon City. The work was sculpted by the Filipino artist Luis “Junyee” Yee Jr. It’s a work of triangles and open doors, signifying the “courage and humanitarian deeds of the Filipino people in welcoming the Jews who escaped the Holocaust in Europe in 1939.” Like in many other places in the world, there is a large Filipino workforce in Israel. They consist mostly of caregivers for the elderly and housekeeping staff in hotels. Much of the community’s life revolves around local Christian churches. Information about community members who are hospitalized or unwell often reaches our consulate, allowing the ambassador to coordinate visits and offer support through the community network. Stories abound about the grit and determination of the Filipino caregivers in Israel. One of them is a quick-thinking caregiver who saved her own life and that of her 95-year-old employer Nitza Hefetz on Oct. 7, 2023, when Hamas terrorists invaded Israel. The Hamas terrorists had broken into Kibbutz Nirim, which was near the border with Gaza. Camille Jesalva gave them $370, which she had saved and would have bought her a return ticket to the Philippines. Camille’s fast thinking on her feet saved her life and that of the old woman she was caring for. Around her, in Kibbutz Nirim, the Hamas terrorists were pulling people from their safe houses, small concrete spaces inside their homes that were supposed to protect them from rockets and missiles. But the doors of these safe houses were unlocked, so that the rescue workers could later pluck the people trapped inside. Babies were beheaded and young women raped. An old woman was strapped to her wheelchair. Gasoline was poured on her. Then, one Hamas terrorist threw a lighted match at her — and filmed her live on Facebook, as she writhed and burned into ashes. To be concluded on Aug. XX, 2026
